Hook: London, July 1858. A few years earlier, Parliament had decided, in the words of the man who now led the House of Commons, that 'the sewage of the metropolis should be diverted to the waters of the Thames'. Now it was summer, and the river ran past Parliament's own windows. On the fifteenth of July, Benjamin Disraeli rose and told the House that the Thames had 'really become a Stygian pool, reeking with ineffable and intolerable horrors'. Almost every living thing in it, he said, had disappeared, and there was 'a pervading apprehension of pestilence in this great city'.

What happened next was fast. Disraeli asked for leave to bring in a bill on the fifteenth of July. On the second of August, the Queen's commissioners told both Houses she had 'readily sanctioned the Act ... for the Purification of that noble River'. Eighteen days. The cost, Disraeli said, 'cannot, indeed, be computed at much less than three million pounds'. It would be paid by a rate of no more than threepence in the pound on London's property, for forty years: a bill, spread over two generations, for pipes meant to last far longer.

Hold that thought: pipes paid for over decades. Now jump to America today, and ask a simple question of each household bill: in how many years since 1953 did its price fall? Water and sewerage: not once in seventy-two years. Rubbish collection, measured since 1984: not once. Rent shares that record. Prices in general fell in 2 years. Electricity fell in 8, and piped gas in 17. The bills nobody thinks about are the ones that have only ever gone one way.

Water comes in through pipes built to last for generations, and leaves through sewers built the same way. Rubbish leaves in a truck and ends in a hole in the ground that nobody wants next door. Industry, Built. Part fourteen: water and waste. Why are the businesses nobody thinks about among the steadiest there are?
Run: Chapter one. Run it: the last landfill in the valley.

You own the only landfill in a valley. It has room for another 30 million tons of rubbish, and every ton costs you about $25 to bury: the compacting, the daily soil cover, the leachate and gas systems, and money set aside for closing it. The valley's own towns make 1.5 million tons a year. The next landfill is over the hills. It charges $45 a ton, and hauling a ton there costs another $20, so the valley will pay you up to $65 before it starts trucking its rubbish away. The towns on the other side would bring you another million tons a year, but only at $45. And someone has applied for a permit to open a rival landfill in the valley. When it opens, you will both charge $45 and split the rubbish.

You have three plans. One: fill it fast. Charge the same as the landfill over the hills, take everybody's rubbish, the valley's and the neighbours', and turn your airspace into cash as quickly as you can. Two: charge the ceiling. Take only the valley's rubbish, at $65 a ton, until the rival opens. Three: charge the ceiling, and also spend $15 million now on applying to expand, which adds 15 million tons of room in year 8. We score each plan the way an owner would: the cash each year, discounted at 7 per cent a year back to today. Pick one before we run it.

Run it, with the rival's permit taking fifteen years. Plan one empties fastest: 2.5 million tons a year at a modest margin. Plans two and three fill slowly, at $40 of margin on every ton. Then the rival opens, the fee falls to $45, and the volume is shared. Plan one is already full, in year 12. The scores: filling fast is worth about $397 million today. Charging the ceiling, about $590 million. And charging the ceiling while you expand, about $623 million. The slow, expensive landfill is worth half as much again as the fast, cheap one.

Now change one thing. Suppose the rival's permit takes five years instead of fifteen. Every plan is worth less. Charging the ceiling falls from about $590 million to $425 million, because the ceiling only lasts five years. The gap between the plans shrinks too: filling fast is worth $361 million, expanding $452. So the most valuable thing you own is not the hole. It is the time it takes anyone else to get permission to dig another: in this valley, ten years of it are worth about $164 million.

Draw it for every permit time. If the rival could open tomorrow, the first two plans are worth exactly the same, about $287 million: airspace with competition next door is just a place to put rubbish. The longer the rival waits, the more the patient plans are worth, and filling fast stops gaining once you would be full before the rival arrives. Divide by the tons, and a ton of room in the ground is worth about $20 today. Waste Management's accounts carry its airspace at about $6.96 a ton, because accounts record what it cost to build, not what scarcity makes it worth. Hold on to that gap; it is the whole business.
System: Chapter two. Water as a system.

A water company sells something that falls from the sky. What it actually owns is a machine for moving it. Water is taken from a river, a reservoir or the ground. It is cleaned: settled, filtered and disinfected. It is stored, often up high, because height is pressure. Then it runs through mains under the street to every home and business. What goes down the drain runs the other way, through sewers, to a works that treats it and returns it to a river. A cubic metre of water weighs a tonne. It is too heavy to move far, so every town has its own pipes, and the company that owns them has no competitor on the street.

That machine is almost all fixed cost, in things that last for decades. Every few years America's Environmental Protection Agency asks the country's water systems what they need to spend over the next twenty years. For drinking water, the answer was about $625 billion. About $423 billion of it, two dollars in every three, is pipes: replacing and repairing the mains under the streets. For sewers, sewage works and storm water, another $630 billion. All of it spread across more than 148,000 public water systems and 17,544 public sewage works, with about 4 million lead pipes still connecting homes to the mains.

Watch what that does to a water company's accounts. This is American Water, which describes itself as the largest regulated water utility in the United States. In blue, what it spends each year on pipes and plants. In grey, what its accounts say wore out. In 2025 it spent about $3.1 billion and used up about $0.9 billion: 3.5 dollars in for every dollar worn out. The pile of assets grows every year. And, as the next chapter shows, a regulated water company is paid a return on exactly that pile.
Regulated: Chapter three. The regulated water company.

Because nobody can compete on the street, someone has to set the price. Regulators do it in different ways; England's is the cleanest to draw. Here is the Works' water company, in round numbers. Its pipes, works and reservoirs are counted in a regulatory asset base: £10 billion. Each year the regulator lets it earn a return on that base, here 4 per cent after inflation: £400 million. It lets it recover a slice of the base itself, as if the pipes were wearing out: another £400 million. And it allows the running costs it thinks an efficient company would have: £600 million. Add them up and divide by the households: £233 a year each. That is the bill.

Now let the company invest. Each year it spends £900 million on new pipes and works, which are added to the base, while 4 per cent of the base is run off. Spending more than runs off, the base grows: from £10 billion to about £18 billion in twenty-five years. And because the bill is built on the base, the bill grows too, from £233 to about £340, before any inflation. This is the engine of every regulated water company: it earns a return on what it has invested, so it grows by investing, and the customers pay for the growth through their bills.

Who gets that return depends on how the base was paid for. Suppose the base earns four per cent a year. If the shareholders paid for all of it, they earn four per cent. Now borrow part of it at two per cent. The lenders get their two, and the shareholders keep the rest of the four on a smaller stake: at 55 per cent debt they earn about 6.4 per cent, at 80 per cent about 12. But if debt costs five per cent, the same borrowing works in reverse: at 80 per cent debt, the shareholders earn about nothing. When England's water companies were privatized, they had little debt. Between 1991 and 2009, their average gearing went from 4 per cent to 72 per cent. While debt is cheap, borrowing turns a steady return into a much larger one for the owners. When it becomes dear, the same borrowing eats the owners' return, and then the company's ability to pay.
England: England is where this model was pushed furthest. In 1989 the government sold its 10 regional water and sewerage authorities as companies listed on the stock exchange, with little debt and a regulator, Ofwat, to set their prices. By 2025 only 3 were still listed. Seven had been bought by private owners, from private equity funds to international infrastructure companies, and Welsh Water is run not for profit. The smaller water-only companies were consolidated from 29 to 5. A steady, inflation-linked return on a monopoly is exactly what long-term investors want to own.

Then came the bill for the pipes. The government and the regulators wanted far more investment: in sewage works and storm overflows, in reservoirs and in mains. For 2020 to 2025, Ofwat had allowed the sector about £62 billion of spending. For 2025 to 2030, about £104 billion, in today's prices. To attract the money, it raised the return it allows on the asset base, from 2.96 per cent to 4.03 per cent after inflation; five companies appealed, and the competition authority gave them 4.20. The average bill for 2025-26 is about £603 a year, of which about £43 is the higher return alone, and Ofwat expects bills to keep rising by about £31 a year before inflation. And because the companies borrowed so much in the cheap years, the Water Commission reckoned they would need £7 to 13 billion of new equity from their owners to pay for it.

The sharpest case is the company that serves the city where this story began. Thames Water has about 16 million customers. When the Water Commission reported in July 2025, it noted that Thames was £16.8 billion in debt, and that Ofwat had just penalized it £141 million over its business plan. In March 2026, a consortium of the company's own lenders proposed to take it over and put in new money. In June, the Environment Secretary told Parliament that the offer did not go far enough to protect customers and the environment. The decision is Ofwat's, and would then need a public consultation and a court. When this film was made, none had been announced. The model that works so smoothly in the Works, a steady return on a growing base, fails when the company is heavily indebted and the next round of pipes has to be paid for.
Elsewhere: Chapter five. Public and private elsewhere.

America does the same arithmetic in fifty different rooms: its investor-owned water companies are regulated by state commissions, one rate case at a time. Here is one from American Water's 2025 report: its Kentucky subsidiary, with a rate base of $667 million. The commission assumed it was paid for 52 per cent by shareholders and the rest by lenders. And it allowed the shareholders a return of 9.70 per cent: about $34 million a year on that slice. England's regulator allows 5.1 per cent after inflation, about seven before it. American Water serves about 14 million people in 24 states, plans to invest 46 to 48 billion dollars over ten years, and has agreed to merge with Essential Utilities, another water company, in a deal it expects to close by early 2027.

Brazil went the other way, recently. Sabesp supplies water to about 30 million people in the state of São Paulo. Until 2024, the state owned about half of it. On the twenty-second of July 2024 it sold most of its shares, keeping 18 per cent, and signed a new concession that pulled forward the deadline for giving 99 per cent of the population water, and 90 per cent sewage treatment, from 2033 to 2029. Watch the investment. About R$6.3 billion in 2023, R$6.9 billion in 2024, and R$15.2 billion in 2025, more than double, with about R$70 billion planned by 2029. Private money, a deadline and a regulated return can build pipes quickly, if the bills can bear it.
Collection: Now the other half: rubbish. Collection is a truck, a crew and a route. The truck costs much the same each day whether it stops at a hundred bins or a thousand. What it sells is stops, and the time between stops is wasted. On a street where one hauler has every house, the truck pulls up, tips a bin, rolls a few metres, tips the next. In the Works' version, that comes to about $1.10 a stop. Now split the street between two haulers, taking alternate houses. Each truck still drives the whole street, but stops half as often. Each pays about $1.24 a stop: the same street, served twice, at a higher cost to everyone.

Draw the cost per stop against the hauler's share of the street. With every house, about $1.10. With half, about $1.24. With a tenth, more than two dollars. Suppose the going price is $1.37 a stop. One hauler with the whole street makes about $275 a day. Two haulers make about $116 each, much less than half as much between them. Three lose money. So the street tends to end up with one truck: either the town grants one hauler the whole district, or the haulers buy each other's customers until one is left. Density is the moat.

And the price? America's consumer price index for rubbish collection has doubled since 1984 after allowing for inflation: about 2.0 times. Here is the biggest hauler, Waste Management, with about $25 billion of revenue in 2025, after taking out what its own trucks paid its own landfills. Collection is the bulk of it, about $15 billion, from businesses, factories and homes. Its contracts with customers, it says, carry yearly price changes linked to the consumer price index, fuel or other costs. That is the steadiness: a price that follows costs up, on a route nobody else can serve as cheaply.
Landfill: Chapter seven. The hole in the ground.

Every truck ends at a hole in the ground, and the hole is the most valuable thing in the business. A modern landfill is not a dump. Since 1991, the standard design for a new American landfill looks like this. At the bottom, at least 2 feet of compacted clay. On top of it, a plastic membrane, 60 thousandths of an inch thick if it is polyethylene. Above that, pipes to collect the leachate, the liquid that drains through rubbish, so that no more than 30 centimetres of it ever pools on the liner. Then the rubbish itself, compacted in cells and covered with soil at the end of every day. Wells to draw off the gas it gives off as it rots. And when it is full, a cap, and 30 years of monitoring and repairs afterwards, paid for by the owner.

Rules like that are expensive to meet, and small dumps could not meet them. In 1988 America had 7,924 municipal landfills. By 2009 it had 1,908. Yet the tonnage going into them hardly changed: about 143 million tons in 1990, about 146 million in 2018, the last year the EPA counted. Small town dumps closed; big, engineered regional landfills took their place. The average landfill went from about 18 thousand tons a year to about 70 thousand: four times the size.

For the owners, a landfill's room is an inventory, counted in years. Waste Management has 257 landfills. A few dozen have less than ten years of room left; most have more than twenty. Weighted by size, about 38 years. Republic Services counts its airspace in cubic yards. It began 2025 with 4,745 million of permitted space. It bought landfills with another 71 million and won permits for 145 million more. It filled 86 million. It ended the year with more room than it started with. Counting the expansions it expects, it has about 58 years at the rate it fills today. The inventory is not running out; it is being replaced, one hard-won permit at a time.

So the big haulers own the whole chain. The truck collects; a transfer station packs the rubbish into big trailers for the long haul; and the trailer unloads at a landfill the same company owns. About two-thirds of what Republic's trucks collect goes into Republic's own landfills. Waste Management's landfills took in $5.3 billion in 2025, and $1.6 billion of that came from its own trucks. And the price of tipping rose: the national average fee went from about $18 a ton in 1985 to about $49 in 1995, in 2013 dollars, and then stayed there. Owning the hole means a rival hauler, however efficient its trucks, still pays you to tip.
Intermission: An intermission: seventy-two years of American household bills, each divided by prices in general, so that a flat line means the bill kept pace with everything else. Watch them together. Electricity ends about where it started, a little below. Rent barely moves. Piped gas rises and falls with the gas market. Rubbish collection, since its index began in 1984, has doubled. And water and sewerage has risen almost every year for seven decades: 3.7 times as expensive, after inflation, as in 1953. Nothing else on this chart comes close.

In plain numbers: since 1953, prices in general have risen about 12 times. The price of water and sewerage has risen about 45 times. The reason, as the rest of this film argues: a bill built on pipes and works that keep being replaced, and standards that keep being raised. Back to the rubbish, and what happens to the part we try to recycle.
Recycling: What happens to America's rubbish? Here is the EPA's count, from 1960 to 2018, the last year it has published. In 1960 almost all of it was buried or burned. When the EPA sounded its alarm in 1989, it said 80 per cent of garbage was landfilled and only 10 per cent recycled. By 2018, of about 292 million tons, about 24 per cent was recycled and 9 composted; about 12 per cent was burned to make electricity; and still half, 50 per cent, went into the ground. Recycling grew enormously, but it grew alongside landfill, not instead of it.

Recycling is a factory. The blue bin's contents are tipped onto a belt and sorted, by screens, magnets, jets of air and people, into bales: cardboard, paper, aluminium, plastic. The bales are sold to mills and smelters, at whatever the market pays that month. For Republic Services, a ton of its sorted recyclables fetched about $164 on average in 2024, and $135 in 2025; every ten dollars a ton moves its revenue and profit by about $13 million a year. Sorting costs much the same whatever the bales fetch. So when bale prices fall, someone has to pay the difference: the hauler, or the town that hired it.

And they do fall. For years, a significant part of the fibre America's haulers recovered was shipped abroad, particularly to China. Here is the US producer price index for recyclable paper. In 2017 China announced a ban on imports of mixed waste paper and mixed plastics from the first of January 2018, as Waste Management told its shareholders. In the two years that followed, the index fell from about 465 to about 146, by 69 per cent. It has swung just as hard since: back to about 515 at the end of 2021, down to about 188 a year later. When bales fetch less than the sorting costs, recycling costs money instead of earning it. The business that sorts it is a factory exposed to a world market.
Hazard: Chapter nine. Waste the law creates.

Some waste markets exist only because the law forbids the cheap alternative. Under America's main waste law, anyone who treats, stores or disposes of hazardous waste needs a special permit, and each one comes with clean-up duties and proof that the owner can pay for them. So the places that can legally burn a drum of solvent or bury contaminated soil are few. Clean Harbors, the largest such network in North America by its own account, runs 10 commercial hazardous waste incinerators. And 7 commercial landfills, 6 of them licensed for hazardous waste, with about 33 million cubic yards of room left. It describes its permits as hard to come by. A permit that is hard to get is a moat that is hard to cross.

And it has grown. Clean Harbors' revenue was about $1.1 billion in 2009. By 2025, about $6 billion. Medical waste works the same way: rules about how a hospital must get rid of needles and tissue create a business. Waste Management bought Stericycle, a medical waste company, in 2024; in 2025 that arm brought in about $2.5 billion. In waste, the regulator does not just police the market. It draws it.

The law makes costs for water companies too, and this is the newest. In April 2024 America set its first national limits on 'forever chemicals' in drinking water: for the two best known, PFOA and PFOS, 4 parts per trillion. Four parts per trillion is about four seconds in 32 thousand years. The chemical makers have been paying: 3M agreed to pay America's public water suppliers 10.5 to 12.5 billion dollars. The water companies must build the treatment. American Water plans about $4.1 billion over five years on water quality, most of it to comply with environmental rules. Under the rule as written, the deadline is April 2029; the EPA has said it intends to extend it to 2031. Either way, the cost goes into the asset base, and from there into the bill.
Returns: Chapter ten. Why the steady money is bought.

Now the reason investors pay up for all this. Each row is a company; each dot, one year's profit per dollar of revenue since 2010. The water companies: tight clusters, every year well in profit. American States Water never kept less than 15 cents in the dollar or more than 21. The waste companies: a little wider, still almost always in profit; Republic between 5 and 13 cents. Now companies from earlier parts of this series. An oil major, a steelmaker, a chemical company: wider. And a memory-chip maker, an airline and a copper miner: from losses of 72 and 84 cents in the dollar to profits of 28. Same years, same economy. The difference is what the customer can do without.

Three things make these businesses steady, and all three are what a certain kind of owner is looking for. Prices that follow costs: Waste Management's contracts carry yearly price changes linked to the consumer price index and fuel, and England's regulator sets its returns after inflation. Assets nobody can copy: a permitted landfill, or a city's pipes, which would take decades to replace even if anyone were allowed to. And owners who want exactly that. Britain's Water Commission said the industry should attract investors with a 'long-term, low-risk and low-return' approach: pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, infrastructure funds. In England and Wales alone, the regulated water assets are worth about £103 billion. The catch is the one Thames Water showed: borrow too much against a steady business, and the steadiness belongs to the lenders.
World: Everything so far assumes the system exists. For much of the world, it is still being built. The World Health Organization and UNICEF count who has 'safely managed' water, piped or protected, available at home and clean, and safely managed sanitation, where the waste is treated or safely contained. In 2024, about 74 per cent of the world's people had safely managed drinking water, up from 61 per cent in 2000. India went from about 38 to 76 per cent. Sanitation is further behind: about 58 per cent of the world, up from 31. China went from 13 to 69 per cent, India from 9 to 63. In sub-Saharan Africa, about 26 per cent; in Ethiopia, 8. London's problem of 1858 is still, for billions of people, the problem of today, and the pipes and works that solve it are the same slow, heavy, fixed-cost machine.
Landscape: The landscape, as of November 2026, for the companies that file American accounts. The waste haulers are big: Waste Management, about $25 billion of revenue, Republic and Waste Connections behind it, keeping around ten to twelve cents in the dollar. Clean Harbors, the hazardous specialist, and Casella, a smaller hauler, keep less. The water companies are small by revenue, American Water about $5 billion, but keep twenty cents or more in the dollar: a regulated return on a large base of pipes, with little else on the bill. Beyond these: Veolia in Paris, with about €45 billion of revenue from water, waste and energy services; Sabesp in Brazil; the listed English water companies; and thousands of public utilities that own pipes and works of their own.

What to watch. Thames Water, and whether Ofwat accepts its lenders' plan. England's bills, rising every year to 2030. The merger of the two biggest water companies on our chart. Airspace: each year, do the haulers win more permitted room than they fill? The price of a bale of paper, which has more than halved in a single year. And the price of water in America, which brings us to our call.
Called: The forecast to test is the government's own, from the years of America's 'landfill crisis'. In February 1989 the EPA warned that 'one-third of the nation's landfills will be full by 1991', and that the country was 'running out of space to bury' its rubbish. What happened? The landfills did close: from 7,924 in 1988 to 1,908 in 2009. But the rubbish kept going into the ground, about 139 million tons a year then, about 146 million in 2018, into fewer, bigger, lined landfills. By 2009 the EPA itself wrote that 'at the national level, capacity does not appear to be a problem'. Today Waste Management reports about 38 years of permitted room and Republic about 58. Called it? Half. The prediction about landfills came true; the prediction about space did not, because a scarce permit is a price signal, and the industry answered it by building bigger holes.

Now our own forecast, written down so you can check it. Here is how much America's price index for water and sewerage rose each year. From 2017 to 2021, when inflation was low, between three and four per cent. Since 2022, more than four every year. And in the first nine months of 2026, about 4.9 per cent above the same months of 2025. We think 2027 will be another year above four per cent: the pipes still have to be replaced, and the bill is how they are paid for. Against us: if inflation falls back, the water price tends to follow. We give it 70 per cent, and we will check it against the Bureau of Labor Statistics' figures in January 2028, right or wrong.
Outro: Back to London. The plan for the drains Parliament paid for in 1858 was the work of the Metropolitan Board of Works' engineers, among them Joseph Bazalgette. A century and a half later London needed a new sewer tunnel under the river. In 2015, Ofwat licensed a private company to design, build, finance, operate and maintain it, with the government standing behind it against risks no private investor would take. The company's name: Bazalgette Tunnel Limited.

So, the businesses nobody thinks about. They sell a service delivered through a network nobody can duplicate. Almost all of their cost is fixed, in things that last for decades. The money goes to the return on those things, set by a regulator or by the scarcity of a permit. Density, permits and regulators keep it there. And what moves it is rarely the customer, who cannot do without it, but new rules, the cost of borrowing and, for the recyclers, the price of a bale. That is why they are so steady, and why the bill only ever goes one way. Next time: the factories of Act Three, starting with the most complicated thing humanity makes, the semiconductor.
